segments.expected: Kiva read it at the back of the crowd with Pru beside her and Perrin behind, under the lamp, while the tide went out of the timber pond's black water under the boards. Every one of the twelve lanes had gone to the four that stood higher. The Tarn's first four had stood with Trewin on frosted feet and a reserve at Bridie's place, and had won by a single point and the glass. Halden License had beaten the twenty-fourth six to two. The Ropewalk's seven to nothing stood at the head of the column, alone.

segments.expected: "I didn't," he began, and stopped, because Aske was looking at him over his spectacles with no expression whatever. "At the spur," he said. "Yesterday. The boards. When they carried him up the bank. I took the head of the boards at the lip, for the last two paces. They'd have had to set him down on the stones otherwise." He swallowed. "I knew I shouldn't. I knew it while I was doing it. I'd like it known that I'd do it again."

segments.expected: They were big. Everybody from the Tarn was big, as if the hills grew them on purpose. Their captain was a thin dark girl with a still door, who walked as though the stone under her were a field she knew. The others came behind her: a heavy blade, a Hold with long arms, a catcher with a fresh bandage on one wrist. They stood behind their hurdle and looked down the pen at Seven, and Kiva saw them look at the linen on her right hand, and Pru's ten caps, and Jude's left arm hanging, and Perrin standing outside the pen with his hand pressed to his side.

segments.expected: Then they tried to wait her out. The glass was running and the litter was in the middle and the Tarn's captain stood back and folded her arms, and Kiva understood that the point at the glass would go to whichever half the litter's middle lay in, and the litter's middle was on the line. Pru saw it too. Pru said, very quietly, "Head's ours. Foot's theirs. Middle's on the chalk." Kiva did not move her stance. She could not, without shutting. But she leaned. She leaned from the floor, as Anwen leaned, with her knees bent and her weight down, and let the floor push, and the head of the Commodore went a hand's breadth west under her forearms with a scrape of canvas on stone.

segments.expected: The third thing the Tarn tried was their catcher. He was a small fair boy with a fresh bandage on his wrist, and he came in low on the north side with his ward up at his hip, small, the width of a doormat, and set it under the litter's middle. It was clever. He meant to lift the litter's middle on his tray and walk it back east over the line while Kiva sat on the head. A ward lifts. That is what a catcher's tray is for.
